faq.a: Low iodine reduces thyroid hormone synthesis, leading to increased TSH stimulation and thyroid hypertrophy.
faq.q: Why does iodine deficiency cause goitre?

faq.a: No; chronic adequate intake via diet or iodised salt is required; a single dose may cause transient hyperthyroidism.
faq.q: Can a single dose of iodine correct deficiency?

faq.a: It replaces missing hormone in overt hypothyroidism while iodine repletion restores normal synthesis.
faq.q: What is the role of levothyroxine in iodine deficiency?

exam: What bedside signs would suggest iodine deficiency in a child? — Palpable diffuse goitre, delayed growth, poor school performance.
How would you differentiate endemic goitre from Hashimoto thyroiditis? — Check TSH/T4, look for anti‑TPO antibodies, and consider epidemiology.
A pregnant woman from a rural area presents with goitre; what is your immediate management? — Start iodised salt, obtain TSH/free T4, give levothyroxine if hypothyroid.
Why is universal salt iodisation preferred over supplementation tablets? — Ensures population‑wide coverage, compliance, and stable dosing.
Interpret a median urinary iodine concentration of 85 µg/L in a community survey. — Indicates iodine deficiency; public‑health intervention needed.
What are the risks of giving excess iodine to a patient with endemic goitre? — Can trigger iodine‑induced hyperthyroidism (Jod‑Basedow phenomenon).
How does iodine deficiency affect neurodevelopment, and what window is most critical? — Impairs fetal brain development; first trimester is most vulnerable.

If thyroid function tests are unavailable, what clinical algorithm would you use to decide on levothyroxine therapy? — Assess goitre size, symptoms (fatigue, cold intolerance), and pregnancy status; treat if overt hypothyroidism is likely.
ai.title: Iodine Nutrition and Deficiency
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis. Deficiency leads to goitre, hypothyroidism, and neurodevelopmental impairment, especially in pregnant women and children. Low-resource settings face endemic goitre due to iodine‑poor soils.

b: Recommended intake: 150 µg/day (adults), 250 µg/day (pregnant/lactating women)
Main sources: iodised salt, dairy, seafood, fortified flour
Goitre: palpable thyroid enlargement, often diffuse
Hypothyroidism: low T4/T3, high TSH
Cretinism: irreversible mental retardation, growth failure
sections.p: Deficiency occurs when intake falls below requirements for >2 months, leading to a spectrum from mild goitre to severe cretinism.

b: Pregnant women: risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight
Children: impaired cognition, reduced school performance
Adults: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance
sections.p: In East African hospitals, endemic goitre remains common where soils are iodine‑deficient and iodised salt coverage is low.
When laboratory tests are unavailable, rely on clinical signs (goitre, bradycardia, dry skin) and dietary history.

t.b: Is thyroid function suppressed or elevated? – High TSH indicates primary hypothyroidism from iodine deficiency.
Is circulating hormone low? – Low free T4 confirms hypothyroidism.
Is recent iodine intake adequate? – Median UIC <100 µg/L suggests deficiency.
Is goitre present and what is its pattern? – Diffuse enlargement supports endemic goitre.

b: Give a short course of levothyroxine for overt hypothyroidism, especially in pregnancy and children.
Educate on dietary sources and encourage use of fortified foods.
Avoid excessive iodine (e.g., kelp supplements) that can precipitate thyrotoxicosis.
sections.p: Treat the deficiency, monitor thyroid function, and address complications.

b: Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto): anti‑TPO antibodies, usually not endemic.
Graves disease: diffuse goitre with hyperthyroidism, not low iodine.
Thyroid nodules/cancer: focal enlargement, not uniform.
sections.p: Other causes of goitre can mimic iodine deficiency.

b: UIC can be normal in recent iodine repletion; repeat after 2 weeks.
Pregnancy lowers TSH reference range; use trimester‑specific cut‑offs.
sections.p: Early iodine deficiency may show normal TSH and T4 despite low intake.

b: Key preventive strategy: universal salt iodisation.
Critical threshold: median UIC <100 µg/L = deficiency; 150–249 µg/L = adequate.
sections.p: Focus on public‑health measures, clinical clues, and interpretation of thyroid function tests.

b: Assuming all goitre is due to iodine deficiency without checking TSH.
Using non‑iodised salt for patients on low‑iodine diets.
Neglecting to treat overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy.
sections.p: Pitfalls often seen in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypothyroidism with myxedema coma (altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia)
Acute airway obstruction from massive goitre
